Every NPC comes out Sarah Chen or Marcus Webb. 680 census-sourced names across 12 demographic pools, weighted to real US population share and rolled fresh every reply. Works anywhere. Start here if you don't know which one you want.

Small-town Iowa doesn't sound like Brooklyn. German, Scandinavian, Polish and Czech surnames — Krueger, Lindqvist, Sedlacek — weighted 85% White with the Hispanic presence real meatpacking towns actually have. Coastal pools removed entirely.

English and Scots-Irish over a 38% Black population, matching rural Mississippi and Alabama. Louisiana French in the mix — Broussard, Thibodeaux, Fontenot. Surnames are multi-generational American, not recent African immigration. That distinction matters here.

Hidalgo County is 92% Hispanic and your NPCs should be too. Tejano surnames — Cantú, Longoria, Treviño, Cavazos, Garza — plus the German-Texan layer nobody remembers to include. Anglo names stay rare, because they are.

Cuban, not Mexican. Cabrera, Betancourt, Valdés, Machado — Barajas and Zavala are gone. Cubans are half of Miami-Dade's Hispanic population and it's 69% Hispanic overall. Haitian names get their own pool with matched given names.

Hispanic here means Puerto Rican and Dominican — Colón, Nieves, Feliciano, Báez, Peralta. Italian, Irish and Ashkenazi surnames lead the White pool. Blended from Bronx and Queens: 42% Hispanic, 17% White. Not the Manhattan you were picturing.

Hispano surnames from families that predate the border — Baca, Montoya, Vigil, Archuleta, Tafoya. The only file where the Navajo pool is on, at 11%, matching Four Corners reality. Census-attested surnames only, no name-generator inventions.

Where the Asian pools finally carry real weight — Chinese, Indian, Filipino, Vietnamese, Korean and Japanese at 36% combined, split into six so you never get Sakura Nguyen. Anchored on Alameda and Santa Clara County numbers.
